title: Repo skeleton built
what: Created the shared project skeleton from the setup prompt: pydantic contract models, example responses for every endpoint, mock routers for all three endpoints, and the clickable mockup as the frontend. Checked that each endpoint returns its example data.
why: Lets all three of us start in parallel against the same contract. Mock mode means nothing needs an API key.

title: Example data follows the formula, not the mockup
what: The mockup shows an overall fit of 63, but the formula in AGENTS.md gives 61 for the same scores and importance values. The example response uses 61.
why: A number must be reproducible from the scores; a figure typed into a mockup is not evidence. The difference was reported to the team.

title: Skeleton merged into main
what: Pull request #1 with the skeleton was merged, so everyone starts from the same main branch.

title: Scoring rules as pure functions (no AI)
what: Implemented overall fit, gap ranking and the signature-trait rule from AGENTS.md as plain functions with unit tests based on the example numbers. Wired them into the mock compare endpoint so changing an importance changes the result, and added a terminal demo to see it.
why: The course asks for an explainable AI contribution; building the scoring first makes every derived number traceable before any model is involved.

title: Weighing is done in code, never by the model
what: The model will only judge single traits. Overall fit, the gap ranking behind the suggested directions, and the signature-trait rule are computed by code from the scores and the importance values the designer set.
why: Anyone can trace a number back to a score and an importance the designer chose; an overall score made up by a model could not be inspected.

title: A trait that cannot be judged is never counted as 0
what: Traits the AI cannot assess (feature not visible, or no judgement returned) get status not_assessable and an empty score, and are left out of the overall fit. If nothing could be assessed the overall fit is empty too.
why: Counting them as 0 would present a gap in the evidence as a flaw in the design.

title: Trait extraction pipeline behind MOCK_MODE=0
what: Built the pipeline that sends the included reference images to a vision model and returns the brand's traits: prompt in its own file, image loading, validation of the model's answer, one retry, clear error messages for the designer. Tested with a fake model, so no key is needed to run the tests.
why: This is the part of the project where the AI contribution is judged, so each step is separate and visible.

title: The vision model is a swappable provider
what: All AI code talks to one small provider function. Which company's model sits behind it is chosen with VISION_PROVIDER in .env and registered in a single file.
why: We had no API key yet and may change model during the project; the prompts, the checks and the tests do not depend on the choice, so models can be compared fairly.

title: The model proposes traits, the code checks them
what: Evidence ids for images that were not sent are dropped, the seen-in count is counted from the evidence instead of taken from the model, low confidence is set below 0.6, and a trait with no valid evidence is removed. An unreadable answer is retried once and then reported as an error.
why: A language model can miscount or cite images that do not exist. No traits are invented to fill a gap, so every trait the designer sees is tied to images that were really sent.

title: Extraction prompt: only the images count as evidence
what: The prompt tells the model to report only what is visible in the supplied images, to need at least 2 images per trait, to describe the product and not the photograph, and to return fewer traits rather than pad the list. Brand keywords and values are given as context, not as evidence.
why: For a well-known brand a model could recite textbook traits the designer cannot check against their own reference set.

title: Scoring merged into main
what: Pull request #2 with the scoring rules was merged.

title: Departures stay when a trait's importance is 0
what: A trait set to importance 0 no longer counts in the overall fit and generates no direction, but its departure is still listed. The interface should show it greyed out and let the designer hide it.
why: The AI measures and the designer decides: 'this does not matter to me' should not delete an observation, only stop it from steering the score and the suggestions.

title: Gemini connected as the first vision provider
what: Wrote the connection to Google's Gemini over plain HTTPS (no extra package), asking for JSON output, with the API key sent in a header and never in the web address.
why: A free API key is available through Google AI Studio and no new dependency was needed.

title: Chosen model was closed to new accounts (404)
what: The first default model answered 404 ('no longer available to new users'). Asking the key which models it can use showed newer ones; the default was switched and an unavailable model now gets a clear message.
why: Model names change often, so the code now explains the situation instead of showing a vague error.

title: Gemini often busy (503): automatic retry added
what: The newest model often answered 'high demand' (503) or timed out. The connection now waits 3 and 8 seconds and tries up to three times; other errors are not retried.
why: Busy errors are temporary on Google's side; the designer should not have to press the button again.

title: First real extraction: 12 product screenshots
what: Ran extraction on 12 screenshots of a real brand's products (kept on one laptop, not in the repository). The model found 6 traits in 24 seconds, all with valid evidence ids; a spot check of 2 images found the evidence plausible. Every confidence value was 0.85 to 0.95 and every suggested importance 75 to 95.
why: Shows the pipeline works end to end on real images, and that the model's confidence does not tell traits apart.

title: Repeated extraction: results are not repeatable
what: The same 12 images gave 6 traits in one run and 5 in the next, with reworded names. Four runs showed that the images cited for the strong traits stayed the same while the names and the weaker traits changed.
why: Extraction is a proposal for the designer to edit, not a measurement; a trait found in every run is a stronger candidate. Running it several times inside the product would multiply the API calls, so it stays a team decision.

title: Trait extraction merged into main
what: Pull request #4 with extraction and the Gemini connection was merged.

title: Proposal: send reference images with the compare request
what: Found that the compare request cannot carry the reference pictures: the package stores only image ids, and the backend has no database and may not keep scraped images. Proposed an optional reference_images field on the request. The team agreed.
why: Judging a design against real reference pictures is easier to inspect than judging it against text only. Rejected: image links inside the package, images sent per trait, and keeping images in the server's memory.

title: Design comparison behind MOCK_MODE=0
what: The model judges each trait of an uploaded design (score, status, one-sentence note) in one request. Code decides everything else: skipped traits become not assessable, a score of 70 or more is a match, below 50 a departure, and the overall fit follows from the scores. Directions stay empty until the next milestone.
why: Keeps the AI's job small and checkable.

title: The model never sees the importance values
what: The compare prompt gives each trait's name and description but never its importance.
why: The model cannot bend its scores towards what the designer cares about; the weighting stays visible and editable in one place.

title: One request for all traits, not one per trait
what: All traits are judged in a single request, each with its own judgement in the answer.
why: Fewer calls fit the free quota and fail less often when the model is busy. One request per trait stays an option if the scores look sloppy.

title: Free-tier rate limit blocks the sketch tests
what: Comparing three hand-drawn product sketches against the brand's traits failed repeatedly with 'too many requests' on the main model, over about six minutes of retries, while a smaller model from the same family still answered. (time approximate)
why: Limits are per model, so development can go on with a smaller model; the daily quota also resets overnight.

title: Developer test page for the compare step
what: A page served by the AI core where you load a package, upload a design, move importance sliders and see score bars, matches and departures. Departures of importance-0 traits are greyed out with a hide option.
why: The real screen is not connected to the backend yet; this lets us see and demonstrate real results.

title: A Pro app subscription does not cover the API
what: The Gemini app subscription does not include API use: Google treats them as separate products. The API has its own free tier (content may be used to improve Google's products) and a prepaid paid tier with a $5 minimum. (time approximate)
why: Budget has to be planned separately. A typical run costs cents, but a spending cap should be set before paying.

title: Shrinking images before sending saves nothing
what: Measured one drawing at 2048, 768 and 384 pixels wide: the image cost 1,100 input tokens each time. Google's image-resolution setting cut it to 264. No image library was added. (time approximate)
why: Gemini charges a fixed amount per image whatever its pixel size, so the lever is the resolution setting; the trade-off is less visible detail. A new package would have needed the team's approval anyway.

title: Shared timeline: same format, master page
what: Defined one CSV format for everyone's timeline, a checker, a prompt for teammates to write theirs after the fact, and a web page that merges the files into a master flowchart and refreshes itself.
why: Gives the team and the teachers one visual story of how development went, built from each person's own record.

title: First sketch tests: honest on colour, shaky on transparency
what: Compared three pencil sketches of new product ideas against five traits taken from one real brand's screenshots (kept local). The two colour and material traits, the most important ones, came back as not assessable on all three sketches with no invented score; the notes were concrete. Overall fit was 41, 50 and 58. The transparent-enclosure trait was scored inconsistently (5, 10 and 85), which pencil drawings cannot really show.
why: Confirms the main honesty rule works on real sketches, and shows the overall fit must be shown with how much of the total importance could be judged. Next: tighten the prompt for material traits and repeat a sketch to see how much scores move.

title: The fit is shown with how much importance could be judged
what: Added a coverage figure: the share of the designer's total importance that the AI could actually judge. On every test sketch it was 39%, because the colour, material and transparency traits cannot be seen in pencil. Screens should show the fit as 'based on 39% of the importance'. A contract proposal for an optional coverage field was written.
why: A fit of 45 built on 39% of the importance is not comparable with a 45 built on all of it; without the figure the number would look more solid than it is. Alternative rejected: leaving it to each screen to explain.

title: Stricter prompt: transparency and slot-vs-hole scoring fixed
what: After adding two prompt rules (judge colour, material and transparency only with a clear cue; a different form from the one named is a deviation), the same three sketches gave transparency as not assessable instead of 5, 10 and 85, and slots scored 30 instead of 90. Three repeated runs of one sketch gave identical scores, but an earlier separate run differed by 15 points on one trait.
why: The rule about honest gaps now also covers the weaker cases. The prompt may now be too strict for a sketch that outlines inner parts; that is left to the designer to judge.

title: Suggested directions from the biggest gaps
what: A second model request words up to 3 concrete design directions for the traits with the largest gap (importance x distance from the brand). Code picks the traits, checks that each direction names a trait that was sent, orders them by gap and numbers them. Tried on a real sketch: two drawable suggestions, none for traits that could not be judged.
why: Completes the compare result with the part the designer acts on, and keeps the ranking traceable to their own importance values. If this request fails the scores are still returned.

title: Directions: code chooses the traits, the model words them
what: The model sees each gap trait's name, description, score and observation but never the importance, and may only name traits it was given. A directions request that stays unreadable after one retry returns the comparison without directions instead of failing.
why: Keeps the choice of what matters with the designer's numbers and avoids throwing away a good comparison because of the suggestion step. Cost: one extra request per comparison. Rejected: asking for suggestions inside the judging request, which would have changed the tuned scoring prompt.

title: Low image detail finds the same traits as high
what: Added an optional image-detail setting and ran extraction on the same 12 product screenshots at low, medium and high detail, twice each. The five core traits came back at low detail as they did at high; the one odd trait appeared only at medium. Each run took 5 to 7 seconds.
why: Low detail uses about a quarter of the image tokens, so repeated runs and the reference images get cheaper. Caveat: one brand and two runs per level; very fine detail may need a higher setting elsewhere.

title: Agreed contract change applied on its own branch
what: The team's agreed reference_images field was added to the compare request in AGENTS.md and contracts/models.py, on a separate small branch so the shared files get their own review.
why: The contract is shared, so it changes in one reviewed pull request. The field is optional, so nothing breaks for the other two without it.

title: Compare against the brand's reference images
what: When the reference images are sent, up to 3 per trait (12 distinct per request) are downloaded into memory and shown next to the design; the model judges the design only. A reference that cannot be downloaded is skipped; without the field everything works as before.
why: The AI uses the same pictures the designer sees as evidence on the Style DNA screen, which makes the result easier to inspect.

title: Reference images shift scores within the noise
what: Compared three sketches with and without the 12 reference images. Scores moved by 5 to 15 points, no more than the run-to-run noise measured before. On one sketch the perforation trait became not assessable, so the overall fit showed 92 based on only 19% of the total importance.
why: No proof yet that references make the scores more accurate; the gain is inspectability. A high fit built on a small share of the importance is misleading, so screens should warn when coverage is low.

title: Real token costs: a comparison is about 0.2 cents
what: Measured token use on real requests: one extraction on 12 product screenshots took 4,010 tokens in and 733 out (about 0.3 cents); a sketch comparison including directions took 2,221 in and 476 out (about 0.2 cents) on the small model and about 0.8 cents on the larger one. On the larger model, the default thinking added about 1,200 hidden tokens per request.
why: Replaces earlier guesses with measurements: a $5 prepaid budget covers thousands of small-model comparisons or several hundred on the larger model. The larger model also scored one trait 30 points higher than the small one on the same sketch.

title: Cost controls: cheap defaults, ceiling, spending limit
what: The Gemini connection now defaults to low image detail and minimal thinking, caps each request at 8,192 output tokens, records tokens and estimated cost per request in a local ledger, and stops when an optional spending limit in .env is reached. The try scripts print a cost summary per run.
why: A prepaid budget must not be spendable by a bug or a loop. The limit is an estimate from Google's published prices, so it complements, not replaces, the cap in Google AI Studio. Alternative rejected: relying only on the provider's own cap.

title: A design can be compared from up to 4 views
what: The compare request got an optional additional_design_images field. All views go to the model as one design, and a trait is not assessable only when no view shows it. The interface and the test page let the designer add up to 3 more views. A real test with two views worked for about 0.2 cents.
why: Earlier results kept saying a trait needed a side view; more views raise coverage without changing the scoring. It is a contract change and touches Person C's file, so the team reviews both.

title: Agreed contract fields built: skipped, do/don't, coverage
what: After the team meeting the three open proposals were applied: extraction reports the images it could not analyse and returns do/don't rules, and the compare result carries the coverage. Contract, fixtures, backend and tests were updated together; a real run on 12 screenshots gave three rules and reported two undownloadable images with their reasons.
why: The designer sees what the traits rest on, the package's do/don't section gets content, and every screen can show the fit with its coverage without recomputing it.
